title: Sequoia recommendation-service burst profile and cost modeling
content:
Objective:

This doc captures the burst/steady-state benchmarking and cost modeling for Sequoia (customer recommendations service) POC. The ask from the customer: understand behavior during short bursts (10s–5m), steady traffic at 200–1,000 qps, and cost impact of different batching + caching configs. Goal is a pragmatic recommendation for Dedicated pool sizing and a fallback policy for hosted.

Summary / TL;DR:
- Hardware used: 2xA100-80GB (dedicated), 4xA100-40GB (dedicated), hosted equivalent tested on g1-standard clusters.
- Model: redwood-recs-v1 (causal decoder; 8B params, KV-cache friendly, supports FP16/LLM-int8).
- Peak burst finding: short bursts (30–90s) show P95 latency climbs primarily due to token-generation concurrency (KV-cache misses) and crossing inter-instance batching thresholds.
- Recommended Dedicated config (for 200–500 qps typical): 4xA100-40GB with batching target 32 and token budget 512 yields P95 < 250ms and estimated token cost ~ $0.95 / 1k tokens (platform-only). For heavy 1k qps steady workloads, bump to 2xA100-80GB or autoscale with burst reserve.
- Immediate ops change: add a latency-aware routing policy that routes new sessions to warm instances and enables prefix cache for sessionized traffic.

Test notes and constraints:
- Tests were run in customer's staging VPC replica (network latency ~ 6–12ms to region). We intentionally injected synthetic inter-arrival patterns to approximate traffic (Poisson for steady, gamma-distributed bursts for flash).
- Synthetic user requests: short contexts avg 64 tokens input, expected gen 128 tokens (distribution heavy tail to 512). We tested both deterministic and sampling modes (top-p=0.9).
- Workloads: three profiles used: 1) Business-hours steady: 250 qps with 3% variance, 2) Shopping-event burst: baseline 150 qps spiking to 1,200 qps for 60–180s, 3) Background batch embed/refresh: low-priority long gens.

Hardware, software, and runtime settings:
- Dedicated nodes: A100-80GB (2-node config), A100-40GB (4-node config). Hosted run used standardized g4dn-equivalent autoscaler for parity.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v2.9.1 with continuous batching, KV prefix caching enabled when configured, and quantization experiments: FP16 vs int8 static quant.
- Batch config knobs exercised: target_batch_tokens (16, 32, 64), latency_slo_ms (100, 200, 300), queue_timeout_ms (10, 50, 100).

Methodology:
- Ramp tests: linear ramp from 0 to target over 5 minutes; hold steady for 10 minutes to ensure KV warm-up.
- Burst tests: baseline for 5 minutes, then injected spike (10x baseline) for 30s/90s/300s to observe warm-up and cooling behavior.
- Token-level logging collected: per-request token count, per-token CPU/GPU exec time (approx), cache hit/miss at prefix level, batch sizes observed, and cross-instance aggregation stats.
- Cost model: platform compute cost + GPU amortized (based on committed Dedicated monthly rate), plus token cost approximations derived from avg GPU utilization. Not billing-accurate; used internal costing model RE-COST-v3.

Key results (selected):
- Steady-state (250 qps, avg 128 tokens gen):
  - 4xA100-40GB (batch target 32): P50 95ms, P95 210ms, P99 340ms; throughput headroom ~ +30% before queuing dominates. Avg batch size observed ~28 tokens.
  - 2xA100-80GB (batch target 32): P50 80ms, P95 180ms, P99 320ms; slightly better single-request latency due to larger KV memory and fewer cross-instance hops.
  - Cost estimate per 1M generated tokens (platform compute only): ~ $920 (4x40GB), ~ $1,100 (2x80GB) — note: 80GB config yields better latency but higher unit cost because reserved capacity pricing skew.

- Short burst (60s to 180s spike to 1,000–1,200 qps):
  - Immediate P95 spike observed within 5–8s of burst start: P95 went from 210ms -> 1,100ms on 4x40GB when prefix cache cold.
  - When prefix cache pre-warmed (session-affinity + route to warm pool): P95 spike reduced to ~380–420ms and recovered within ~12–20s.
  - Autoscale boot latency (adding extra node) averaged 45–70s (unacceptable for sub-2min bursts).

- Long tail / worst-case (heavy gen requests 512 tokens average):
  - For long-tokens, batching helps but tail latency saturates due to single-request token processing on GPU memory boundary. P95 > 1.8s unless token preemption or priority lanes used.

Observations (operationally relevant):
- Warm KV-cache is the single biggest lever. Sequences with consistent prefixes (session-based recs) benefit from prefix caching dramatically. For customer traffic (sessionized clicks + recent history) enabling prefix cache reduces token work and smooths burst P95 by ~3x in our tests.
- Batching target 32 is a good default for 8B rec model with avg gen 128 tokens; lower batch targets increase latency cost, higher targets hurt burst latency (queueing). Use adaptive batching with latency SLO enforcement.
- Autoscale is effective for sustained increases >3 minutes, but not for short events. For flash events, recommend a reserved burst capacity (warm standby nodes) or a multi-tier serving policy that fails over to lower-cost, faster-start models (quantized/ distilled) with graceful degradation.
- Quantization (int8) reduced avg per-token GPU time by ~18–22% with negligible degradation in top-recall for recommendations, but increased variance in P99; useful as a cost knob for background/internal traffic but not for mainline served sessions without evaluation flags.

Actionable recommendations for customer POC and short-term roadmap:
1) Dedicated sizing: start with 4xA100-40GB for baseline; configure warm standby of 1–2 nodes (same model) reserved for burst absorption. Estimated monthly committed cost vs hosted run leads to break-even at ~7.5B tokens/month.
2) Routing: implement session affinity + warm pool routing; set warm pool targeted at 10% of anticipated peak qps to bridge 30–120s bursts.
3) Runtime defaults: batching target 32, queue_timeout_ms 50, latency_slo_ms 200 for user-facing routes.
4) Fallbacks: prepare a quantized variant (redwood-recs-v1-int8) and an output-length-limited policy (cap to 256 tokens) for emergency overflow. Automate A/B fallback with quality monitoring.
5) Monitoring: add token-level cost dashboards, real-time batch-size histograms, cache hit ratio alert (<65% on sessionized endpoints), and burst-detection alerts that trigger warm pool promotion.

Open questions / risks:
- Customer tight SLAs <150ms P95 will require model distillation or moving to smaller model family — or co-locating inference close to client to eliminate network jitter.
- Billing model assumptions: Dedicated pricing varies by contract; our modeling assumes mid-range committed discounts. Need to validate actual contract numbers before finalizing cost table for finance.
- Cold-start patterns for brand-new sessions (no prefix) still create a measurable P99 spike — need to verify whether synthetic pre-warming (predictive cache seeding) is acceptable for privacy/compliance.

Appendix A — raw sample numbers (selected traces):
- 4xA100-40GB steady 250 qps: mean batch size 28, avg GPU util 65%, tokens/sec 85k, P50 95ms, P95 210ms, P99 340ms.
- 4xA100-40GB burst 1200 qps (cold cache): P95 1,100ms, 30s median recovery to baseline after spike ends.
- 4xA100-40GB burst 1200 qps (warm cache): P95 420ms, recovery 12s.
- 2xA100-80GB steady 250 qps: mean batch size 30, avg GPU util 78%, tokens/sec 92k, P95 180ms.

Appendix B — short checklist for next workshop with customer:
- Bring a validated traffic replay from prod for a 48-hour window (anonymized).
- Run cache-warm vs cold comparison with their session segmentation.
- Show cost break-even slide for Dedicated vs Hosted at multiple token volumes (1B, 5B, 10B tokens).
- Prepare a live fallback demo using int8 variant and length-limited policy.
